faq.question: How long does a typical project take?
faq.answer: Most single-discipline projects run 4–10 weeks; branding is on the shorter end, apps on the longer end. Combined programs (brand + web, for example) usually run 2–4 months. You'll get a specific timeline before anything is signed off.

faq.question: Do you work with early-stage startups, or only established brands?
faq.answer: Both. Early-stage teams tend to lean on the Consultancy and Branding services first; established brands more often come in for a rebrand or a rebuild. Scope flexes to match the stage you're at.

faq.question: What's actually included in maintenance?
faq.answer: Software and plugin updates, uptime and error monitoring, priority bug fixes, and small content or feature changes: the kind of upkeep that otherwise gets put off until something breaks.

faq.question: Do you work with teams outside the UK?
faq.answer: Yes. Most collaboration happens over call and async review, so time zones with a few hours of overlap work fine. We'll flag it early if a project needs more in-person time than that allows.

faq.question: Can we bring you in for just one part, the website say?
faq.answer: Yes. Each of the six services can be booked on its own as a Project engagement. If it later needs a companion piece, a brand to sit behind that website for instance, we can fold it into a Program without starting over.

side: Keep the workshop, rebuild the voice
Fenwick & Ash.lede: Forty years of joinery, rebuilt for a design-forward audience without losing the workshop underneath it.
paras: Fenwick & Ash made beautiful furniture and looked like a phone directory advert. The audit kept everything earned (the name, the heritage, the client book) and cut everything that wasn’t.
The site runs on the same grid. Every project page is a case file: commission, wood, hours at the bench. The team edits it themselves through a CMS handover.
figs: Product photography: one object, one light
quote: “They kept forty years of history and still made us look like the future.”

Loop.lede: A habit tracker people actually keep opening, from onboarding flow to App Store.
paras: Most habit apps are guilt machines. Loop is built around streaks that forgive: miss a day and the line bends, it doesn’t break. That single product decision shaped the whole design system: soft curves, warm darks, one accent.
quote: “D30 retention doubled against the old prototype. The forgiveness mechanic did that.”

Marrow.lede: A direct-to-consumer butchery entering a crowded shelf: named, positioned, dressed.
chapters: Shortlists went from forty names to four to one. “Marrow” won because it’s the part of the animal chefs fight over: depth, richness, the good stuff.
The shelf already shouts “artisanal small-batch”. Marrow is positioned on provenance transparency: farm, distance, days aged, printed on every pack.
The identity is a butcher’s block of a wordmark, blood-red accent, and packaging that reads like a spec sheet. It stands out by standing still.

Northline.lede: A logistics platform rebuilt from the database up, for speed and for the people using it daily.
paras: The old system took eleven seconds to draw a morning board. Dispatchers had memorised workarounds. We rebuilt the query layer first, then the UI around the three questions a dispatcher actually asks: what’s late, what’s empty, what’s next.
quote: “The morning board loads before my coffee does. That’s the whole review.”
